Severity correctly low because the normal write path (validate_license) does normalize, making the bad-value case an edge of an edge.

verified_findings.title: free_port() TOCTOU: bound test port is released before whisper-server binds it
verified_findings.location: src-tauri/src/whisper.rs:552-554 (free_port), used at whisper.rs:145 then spawn at 169
verified_findings.detail: VERIFIED. free_port() (whisper.rs:552-554) is `(BASE_PORT..BASE_PORT+20).find(|p| TcpListener::bind((HOST,*p)).is_ok())` — the listener is a temporary dropped immediately, releasing the port. The child is spawned later in the init thread (spawn_server at whisper.rs:169) and only binds after the model loads (potentially seconds). The startup loop (whisper.rs:194-236) marks Ready on a successful TCP connect (line 202-211) to whatever holds the port — it does not verify the listener is actually whisper-server. The window is real, bounded by the 20-port scan and the generation guards.
verified_findings.recommendation: Option (a): after the TCP connect succeeds in the startup loop, issue a lenient HTTP probe (any HTTP response = a server we spawned) before marking Ready. Smaller and also catches the foreign-listener case. Option (b) is more invasive. Given INFERENCE already POSTs to /inference, a cheap GET to the server root suffices.
verified_findings.impact: Rare: the engine could mark Ready while pointed at an unrelated local listener, causing transcription to fail with a confusing error instead of a clean restart.
verified_findings.risk: Adding an HTTP probe couples to whisper-server responding to some endpoint; keep it lenient (any HTTP status = ours).
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: Identical on both platforms (std::net + spawned binary); no platform branch.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Confirmed at low. The TOCTOU window is genuinely present and the Ready check is a bare TCP connect (line 202) with no protocol verification. Severity correctly low: HOST is localhost-only, the scan range is 20 ports, and a racing second start() is itself serialized by the generation counter, so realistic exploitation/collision is unlikely outside a contended dev box.

verified_findings.title: Silent .ok()/.unwrap_or swallows can lose the license key or trial count with no signal
verified_findings.detail: VERIFIED. trial::save (trial.rs:186-199) calls `settings.save().ok()` (189), `std::fs::write(&secondary,&blob).ok()` (195), and (Windows) write_registry (198) — all three persistence sinks swallow errors and there is ZERO logging in the function. increment_trial_count (main.rs:194-199) returns nothing and the in-memory count advances regardless. On a total-persistence failure, next launch trial::load reads stale max(lifetime_total) from read_all_locations (trial.rs:201-224), effectively returning free dictations — a minor trial-bypass. settings.rs::save (64-70) is correctly atomic (tmp+rename) but its callers (e.g. trial.rs:189) discard the Result. The codebase elsewhere treats this seriously: validate_license logs license save failure (main.rs:141-143).
verified_findings.recommendation: Add a single warn! in trial::save when ALL sinks fail (track each .ok() into a bool; if none succeeded, log). Diagnosability only; do not fail dictation. No control-flow change.
verified_findings.impact: Trial accounting can silently drift on storage failure (minor revenue/integrity) and the failure is undiagnosable because nothing is logged at the save site.
verified_findings.risk: None — logging only.
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: Registry write is Windows-only and cfg-gated (trial.rs:197-198); the settings.json + secondary-file sinks are cross-platform, so both OSes retain ≥2 sinks. Logging change is platform-agnostic.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Confirmed at low. Verified all three .ok() sinks and the absence of any log line in trial::save. The trial-bypass mechanism is real but requires all sinks to fail simultaneously (disk full / locked-down ACLs across LocalAppData + data_dir + registry), which is rare — hence low. The recommendation is correctly scoped to logging only, so it can't introduce a regression on either platform.

verified_findings.title: WhisperEngine::transcribe restart path re-reads model_file under a fresh lock — racy model preference
verified_findings.detail: VERIFIED. On the failed-engine restart branch transcribe does `let model = self.inner.lock().model_file.clone();` (whisper.rs:314), drops the lock, derives pref, then calls self.start(pref). The inference-retry branch repeats this at line 328. A concurrent set_setting('whisper_model')/language change (main.rs:117,122) also calls reload→start, bumping generation (whisper.rs:152). The generation logic correctly abandons the loser's init thread, so this is mostly benign, but transcribe's pre-lock model_file snapshot can be stale relative to the start() it triggers, so one transcription could restart on the OLD model right after the user picked a new one. Self-corrects next dictation.
verified_findings.recommendation: Pass pref=None on the restart so resolve_model re-derives from current settings/state rather than the pre-lock snapshot (resolve_model already falls back to best-available). Smallest safe change; applies to both the wait_ready-restart (line 316) and the post_inference-retry (line 330) branches.
verified_findings.impact: A transcription that triggers a restart immediately after a model change may run once on the previous model; self-corrects on the next dictation.
verified_findings.risk: None — pref=None has well-defined fallback behavior.
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: Platform-independent engine logic.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Confirmed at low. The stale-snapshot window is real (lock dropped between read and start), but the generation counter makes it self-healing and the only consequence is one transcription on the prior model. Note the same pattern exists in BOTH restart branches (314 and 328); the fix should cover both, which the recommendation now states. Correctly trivial/low.

verified_findings.title: CSV export: numeric Duration/Words fields are unquoted; text/quote/newline escaping is actually adequate
verified_findings.detail: PARTIALLY VERIFIED — the original framing overstated the gap. The CSV branch DOES double quotes (`t.text.replace('"', "\"\"")`, db.rs:233) and DOES strip both newline chars (`.replace('\n', " ").replace('\r', "")`), so embedded-newline AND embedded-quote breakage are NOT possible for the Text field — that part is RFC-4180-adequate, contrary to the original title. The genuine residual gaps are: (1) Duration and Words are written RAW/unquoted (db.rs:234-235) so a NaN/inf duration would emit a bare token breaking the column — but duration_seconds is an f64 from get_wav_duration and is not NaN/inf today (the finding concedes this); (2) `t.timestamp.get(..19)` (db.rs:232) byte-slices, returning None→full string on any non-ASCII/short value, but timestamps are RFC3339 ASCII (db.rs writes them). Both gaps are purely hypothetical with current data.
verified_findings.recommendation: Low priority. If hardening: format duration with fixed precision (`{:.1}`) so a non-finite value can't break the column, or adopt the `csv` crate for the branch. The quote/newline handling already in place needs no change.
verified_findings.impact: No real data-quality issue with current transcript content; the unquoted numeric fields are only a theoretical risk if duration ever became non-finite.
verified_findings.risk: Low; csv crate is well-established if adopted.
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: Platform-independent.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Adjusted (not rejected) because there IS a narrow real gap (unquoted numeric fields), but the original title/detail claimed the export 'does not RFC-4180-escape embedded newlines/quotes fully' — code review shows quotes ARE doubled and newlines ARE stripped, so that specific claim is wrong. Downgraded the framing to the one defensible residual. Borderline-reject; kept as adjusted-low because the numeric-field point, while not triggerable today, is a legitimate robustness nit in a user-facing export.

verified_findings.title: spawn_server passes model path via to_string_lossy — a non-UTF8 data dir path would corrupt the -m argument
verified_findings.detail: VERIFIED. spawn_server (whisper.rs:497-498) builds args with `cmd.args(["-m", &model.to_string_lossy(), ...])`. to_string_lossy replaces invalid UTF-8 with U+FFFD, so a Windows profile path with non-UTF8 bytes (rare, legacy code-page profiles) would hand whisper-server a corrupted path and fail with a misleading 'model not found'. Command::arg accepts OsStr/AsRef<OsStr> directly, so the lossy conversion is avoidable.
verified_findings.recommendation: Build incrementally: `cmd.arg("-m").arg(model)` (model is &Path, which is AsRef<OsStr>) instead of the str-array form. Preserves the OsStr losslessly to the child process.
verified_findings.impact: Rare (non-UTF8 profile path) but produces a confusing failure; cheap to make correct.
verified_findings.risk: None — OsStr is the correct type for process args.
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: More likely on Windows (legacy code-page profile names) than macOS (UTF-8 filesystem); fix is identical and platform-agnostic. Note whisper-server itself must accept the path arg as given — on Windows args are passed as UTF-16 so OsStr round-trips losslessly to the child's wide-char argv.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Confirmed at low. The lossy conversion is real and avoidable. Severity correctly low: it only bites a non-UTF8 user-profile path, which is genuinely rare on modern Windows and effectively impossible on macOS's UTF-8 filesystem. The fix is the idiomatic OsStr-preserving form and carries no behavior change for ASCII paths (the overwhelming majority).

verified_findings.title: text_cleanup recompiles ~70 regexes per clean() call instead of memoizing like the file's other Lazy regexes
verified_findings.detail: VERIFIED. fix_acronyms (text_cleanup.rs:261-264) compiles a fresh `Regex::new(...).unwrap()` per ALWAYS_UPPERCASE entry per call; the list has ~50 entries (text_cleanup.rs:24-30). apply_informal_corrections compiles 11 per call (line 277), tighten_phrasing 7 (line 295) — ~68 compilations. Confirmed clean()'s gating: fix_acronyms runs at standard+aggressive, the other two only at aggressive (clean(), lines 83-94), so the full ~68 hits only aggressive mode. Confirmed clean() runs inside spawn_blocking (main.rs:413), off the UI thread, and whisper response is bounded to 50MB (whisper.rs:540) — so this is wasted CPU, not user-blocking latency. The file already uses the right pattern (Lazy<Vec<Regex>> at text_cleanup.rs:45-53).
verified_findings.recommendation: Precompile these sets once via once_cell::Lazy (e.g. Lazy<Vec<(Regex, &str)>> for the corrections, Lazy<Vec<Regex>> for acronyms) exactly like RE_HALLUCINATIONS. Matches the file's existing idiom; measurable CPU savings on aggressive-mode transcripts.
verified_findings.impact: ~68 regex compilations per aggressive-mode transcription; not user-visible latency (post-transcribe, off-thread) but avoidable CPU/battery, mattering more on macOS laptops.
verified_findings.risk: None — pure memoization of already-correct regexes.
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: Platform-independent CPU cost; matters slightly more on battery-powered macOS devices.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Confirmed at low. Verified the per-call compilation in all three functions and the ~50-entry ALWAYS_UPPERCASE list, so the '~70 per call' figure is accurate for aggressive mode. Severity correctly low: it runs off the UI thread in spawn_blocking, so it never touches the hotkey/beep latency path the dimension is most worried about — it is pure efficiency, not robustness.

verified_findings.title: is_activated() re-reads token from disk and re-verifies Ed25519 on every require_license call (hotkey path)
verified_findings.detail: VERIFIED. is_activated (activation.rs:20-31) does fs::read_to_string(activation.jwt) + machine_fingerprint() (now memoized via OnceLock, good) + verify_token (full Ed25519 verify, base64 decode, JSON parse, exp check — activation.rs:33-72). require_license (main.rs:173-192) calls is_activated at line 180, and start_recording calls require_license on the hotkey path (main.rs:269). For an activated user this re-reads + re-verifies the token on every dictation start. Confirmed the fingerprint dependency is memoized, so only the file read + Ed25519 verify remain — sub-millisecond, far smaller than the seconds-scale fingerprint bug.
verified_findings.recommendation: Cache the activation result after first successful verify (OnceLock<bool> or short-TTL keyed on token file mtime), invalidating on activate_online/deactivate. Lowest priority of the family; the check_license refresh thread (main.rs:227-235) rewrites the token, so any cache must key on mtime or use a short TTL to avoid serving a stale 'not activated'.
verified_findings.impact: Small per-dictation overhead (one small file read + one Ed25519 verify) on the latency path for every activated user; imperceptible individually but on the critical path and avoidable.
verified_findings.risk: Cache invalidation must cover deactivate AND the background token refresh (check_license:227); mistuned invalidation could brick an activated user mid-session. Keep TTL short or key on file mtime.
verified_findings.dual_platform_note: Platform-independent (std::fs + ed25519-dalek); the underlying fingerprint it depends on is already memoized on both platforms.
verified_findings.skeptic_note: Confirmed but flagged as the weakest of the family. Verified is_activated does read + Ed25519 verify per call on the hotkey path — but Ed25519 verification is microseconds and the token file is tiny, so the magnitude is nowhere near the fingerprint bug (which was seconds of process spawns). I'd rank this lowest-priority: the caching it proposes adds real invalidation risk (the refresh thread at main.rs:227 rewrites the token) for a sub-millisecond win. Keep at low; do NOT prioritize over finding 1 or 2.
